title: Shipwrecks as Cultural–Ecological Systems in Marine Protected Areas: Lessons from Uruguay
content: The Atlantic coast of Rocha, Uruguay, contains more than 200 documented shipwrecks, many located within or adjacent to Marine Protected Areas (MPAs). While Uruguay has made significant progress in marine biodiversity conservation, underwater cultural heritage (UCH) remains largely absent from environmental governance, creating a critical gap as tourism intensifies along this highly dynamic coastline. This research examines how UCH can be integrated into MPA management by framing shipwrecks as components of maritime cultural landscapes, where cultural, ecological, and social processes are deeply intertwined. Drawing on a case study of the Ro-cha coast, the study combines archaeological evidence, ecological data, and analysis of local community engagement and tourism practices. The coastline’s shifting dunes, erosion, and storm events periodically expose and re-bury archaeological remains, while shipwrecks simultaneously function as cultural sites, community reference points, and biodiversity hotspots acting as artificial reefs. These overlapping values highlight a governance paradox: ecosystems receive formal protection, yet cultural heritage is left vulnerable to unregulated access, artifact removal, and informal tourism activities. The paper argues that principles of the UNESCO 2001 Convention on the Protection of the Underwater Cultural Heritage— particularly in situ preservation, non-commercialization, and knowledge-based public access—can guide integrated management even in the absence of formal ratification. By aligning heritage management with the objectives of the UN Ocean Decade (2021–2030), the study indicates how UCH can enrich MPA interpretation, support sustainable and low-impact tourism, and foster community participation in stewardship. The findings highlight the policy relevance of treating marine biodiversity, cultural heritage, and tourism as a single management system to achieve more inclusive, resilient, and inspiring ocean governance.
